Likewise, Grubert and Eimer (2020) attributed capture by the current distractorcolored probes to the activation of a potential target template. Thus, direct neural evidence for distractor template pre-activation remains limited.

The present RSPP addressed this issue by comparing N2pc components elicited by task-irrelevant probes that either matched the distractor color or a neutral color. In distractor match blocks, the distractor color was the only constant informative color across trials, making its use necessary.

Although distractor-colored probes elicited a robust N2pc at the final probe, this response did not differ from that to neutral probes and was therefore not distractor-specific. Instead, the late N2pcmay reflect a general increase in probe-elicited attentional selection as search onset approached.

Because the number of probes was fixed, the final probe may signal imminent search onset, making temporal expectation a plausible explanation. This speculation is compatible with evidence that the timing of N2pc for target-colored probes varies with the expected search onset (Grubert & Eimer, 2018).

N2pc responses to distractor-colored probes were reduced across block halves, particularly at the final probe. Similar reductions following learned distractor regularities have been linked to decreased need for distractor inhibition after search onset, as indexed by reduced P D amplitudes (Hanne et al., 2025; van Moorselaar et al., 2020; van Moorselaar & Slagter, 2019; Wang & Theeuwes, 2018). However, our effects concerned preparatory probe-elicited N2pc rather than post-display Pᴅ. More critically, the present changes did not differ between distractor-colored and neutral probes. Therefore, they cannot be attributed specifically to distractor template learning and may instead reflect more general repetition-related processes, such as reduced responsiveness to task-irrelevant probes. Overall, we thus found no convincing evidence for distractor template pre-activation.

Rethinking the mechanisms of distractor handling

Former research has shown that a salient distractor can elicit an early positivity, often appearing before or overlapping with the N2pc time window (e.g., Gaspar & McDonald, 2014; Sawaki & Luck, 2010). This distractor positivity (i.e., early P D ) has sometimes been interpreted as an index of active suppression, with larger positivities reflecting more efficient suppression (Feldmann-Wüstefeld & Vogel, 2019; Gaspelin et al., 2023; Gaspelin & Luck, 2018). We observed an early distractor positivity (120-200 ms) in both target match and distractor match blocks. Although positivity was larger in distractor match blocks, this effect did not interact with display layout, indicating that the early positivity was not specifically tied to the instructed distractor color. The response therefore provides little evidence for template-specific suppression and is more consistent with a general salience-driven encoding response, such as the Ppc (Barras & Kerzel, 2016; Corriveau et al., 2012; Fortier-Gauthier et al., 2012; Jannati et al., 2013; McDonald et al., 2023), although an overlapping inhibitory contribution cannot be excluded.

In the later time window (220-400 ms), distractors elicited a larger N2pc in distractor match than target match blocks. This pattern is consistent with the reactivation account proposed in the introduction, in which a distractor representation may remain activity-silent during preparation and be reactivated when a matching distractor appears. The distractor acts as a retrieval cue that increases attentional selection. However, this possible reactivation did not support any forms of suppression. Specifically, if suppression had been exclusively engaged, the distractor N2pc should have been absent in distractor match blocks. Alternatively, if the template had supported a "search and destroy" (Moher & Egeth, 2012) account, the enhanced N2pc should have been followed by a stronger P D , reflecting a later suppression (i.e., late P D ) following capture. Neither pattern was observed. Instead, distractor foreknowledge was associated with a larger distractor N2pc without a subsequent P D . Thus, the findings provide little support for either "suppression only" or "search and destroy" accounts.

Taken together, distractor foreknowledge appeared to alter attentional selection only after search onset, and increasing rather than preventing capture by the anticipated distractor.

Enhanced efficiency of target templates

Behavioral performance was substantially better when participants knew the target color than when they knew the distractor color, consistent with previous work showing an advantage of positive over negative cues (Arita et al., 2012; Carlisle, 2023; Conci et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2022; Zhang & Carlisle, 2023). In line with these findings, an earlier target N2pc was observed for target match blocks (220-300 ms) than for distractor match blocks (320-400 ms), which is also consistent with previous reports of faster or larger target N2pc following positive than negative cues (Berggren & Eimer, 2021; Carlisle & Nitka, 2019; Salahub & Emrich, 2021). The use of distractor information may be less efficient because they require additional interpretation and executive control before guiding attention (Chidharom & Carlisle, 2023; de Vries et al., 2019; Rajsic et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020; Zhang & Carlisle, 2023).

The N2pc responses to preparatory probes further demonstrate a difference between foreknowledge of target and distractor information. Target-colored probes triggered a larger N2pc than distractorcolored probes, suggesting that the color information was used selectively. This selectivity also argues against nonspecific feature-priming, which should affect both informed colors similarly. In addition, target-colored probes triggered a larger N2pc than neutral probes starting from the first probe onward, whereas distractor-colored probes, triggered an N2pc only at the final probe and did not differ from neutral probes. Thus, target but not distractor information showed clear evidence of sustained template-specific pre-activation.

Notably, this sustained target-template pre-activation differs from Grubert and Eimer (2018 , 2020 , 2023) who found N2pc elicited by target-colored probes only shortly before search onset, suggesting more transient mode of pre-activation. This discrepancy might be due to different settings of the stimulus-onset asynchrony (SOA) between two subsequent search displays. Their fixed inter-search SOA caused early probes to follow the preceding search almost immediately (i.e., 50 ms), potentially overlapping with decision and response processes, therefore participants might not have been ready for the next trial's template pre-activation at first few probes. In our study, the next trial began only after a response had been made, which may have allowed the template preparation to begin earlier.

However, target template pre-activation may still be strategically timed, as Grubert and Eimer (2018) showed that the N2pc elicited by target-colored probes was delayed when search onset was expected later. Thus, temporal expectations may regulate when target templates become active.

Experience-related changes in attentional selection

The present findings demonstrate that repeated exposure also influenced search efficiency.

Behaviorally, responses became faster across block halves, particularly in distractor match blocks, suggest that participants became more efficient as the distractor color repeated. At the neural level, greater reductions in the N2pc elicited by distractor-colored probes was associated with an attenuated distractor N2pc during search. Thus, reduced preparatory attention to distractor features predicted less later capture. No comparable relationship emerged for target templates, possibly because targetbased selection was already efficient and therefore less susceptible to experience-related improvement.

These findings also align with the contingent capture framework (Folk et al., 1992; Folk & Remington, 1998), according to which attentional capture depends on whether a stimulus matches the current attentional set. Such contingencies can themselves be shaped by experience and repetition (Chelazzi et al., 2019; van Zoest et al., 2021; Vatterott & Vecera, 2012). Our results extend this account by demonstrating that preparatory attentional responses to distractor features can be adaptively tuned with experience to reduce unwanted distractor capture during search.

Conclusion

In conclusion, the present study provides no convincing evidence that distractor templates are preactivated during preparation. Nevertheless, distractor foreknowledge influenced attentional selection after search display onset. And this influence may be adjusted through experience-dependent changes in attentional processing.
